title: Let AI Write the Boring First Draft
summary: AI is great at turning scattered notes into a plain first draft people can argue with. How to brief it, why plain beats polished and what the human pass must check.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
You've explained the same idea in three meetings. Everyone nodded every time. Nobody wrote it down, so now it lives in four people's heads, a Slack thread and a photo of a whiteboard. The idea isn't the hard part anymore. The hard part is the first page: turning scattered notes into a version plain enough that people can point at it and say "this bit's wrong."

AI is surprisingly good at that job, as long as you ask for the boring version. This post covers why boring works, how to brief the model and what you still have to do yourself. For the bigger picture of where AI drafts fit into a codebase, see letting AI draft while humans keep the map.

Why the first page is the hard part

A blank page is expensive in a sneaky way. Nobody can react to it, so the discussion stays vague, and whoever owns the doc keeps postponing it because it feels like a chore.

A plain first pass changes that. The team gets a page to work on. People can point at a paragraph, delete a weak claim, add a missing example and argue about the order. The draft doesn't need to be right to be useful. It needs to be specific enough that disagreeing gets cheap.

Research backs up the speed part. In an MIT experiment with 453 college-educated professionals doing writing tasks matched to their jobs, the group given ChatGPT finished about 40% faster, and their work was rated 18% higher in quality (Noy and Zhang, Science, 2023). The more interesting finding is how the work changed shape: people spent less time on rough drafting and more on coming up with ideas and editing (the working paper). That's the trade this post is about. Let the model take the rough draft, and put your time into the ideas and the edit.

Why boring beats brilliant

It's tempting to ask for the brilliant version: the polished memo, the clever name, the finished plan. Resist it, for two reasons.

First, polish hides weak spots. Smooth sentences make a shaky claim sound settled, and nobody wants to tear up something that already reads like the final version. A plain draft invites correction.

Second, a draft with opinions nudges yours. In a 2023 study, 1,506 participants wrote a short post on whether social media is good for society, some of them with an AI writing assistant set up to argue one side. The assistant shifted the opinions people expressed in their writing, and it moved their answers on a later attitude survey too (Jakesch et al., CHI 2023). A draft that takes a stance before you've decided can end up making the decision for you. Ask for structure first and save the conclusions for later.

What a boring first pass looks like

Headings in a sensible order. Every claim from your notes on its own line. Open questions written as questions. Assumptions labeled as assumptions. No adjectives doing persuasion work.

Brief it like a new teammate

Without context, a model fills gaps with fluent generalities. Give it what a new teammate would need:

  • Source material: the notes, the thread, the transcript. Paste them in rather than describing them.
  • Audience: who reads this and what they already know.
  • The decision it supports: "we have to pick A or B by Friday" focuses a draft far better than "write a design doc."
  • Constraints: length, format, what's out of scope.
  • Permission to leave holes: tell it to write [TODO] instead of inventing a detail.
Turn these notes into a plain first draft of a design note.
Audience: backend team, knows the billing service well.
Decision: retry inside the worker or move retries to a separate queue.
Sections: context, options, trade-offs, open questions.
Use only facts from the notes. Label assumptions as ASSUMPTION.
Where a detail is missing, write [TODO] instead of guessing.
Plain language. No recommendation yet.

The human pass

The draft is raw material, with no authority of its own. Once it exists, your job gets sharper:

  • Which claims are backed by the sources, and which just sound confident?
  • Are the examples real, or did the model invent a plausible one?
  • Which trade-off got smoothed over and needs saying out loud?
  • What's missing that only someone on the team would know?
  • What shouldn't be published at all?

Take this pass seriously, because the line between what AI does well and what it does badly is jagged. In a Harvard Business School and BCG experiment with 758 consultants, people using GPT-4 on tasks inside its abilities completed 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, with results rated more than 40% higher in quality. On a task picked to sit just outside those abilities, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to reach the right answer than those working without it (Dell'Acqua et al., 2023). The tasks looked about equally hard. How good a draft looks tells you nothing about which side of the line you're on. For more on treating output as something to verify, see treating AI suggestions as draft evidence.

Where the boring first pass shines

Some everyday documents are a great fit, because the structure is predictable and the facts already exist somewhere:

  • PR descriptions: feed it the diff and the ticket, get back what changed, why and how to test it. You check the "why."
  • Meeting summaries: decisions, owners, open questions. You check that the decisions were really made.
  • Design note outlines: context, options, trade-offs. You add the trade-off nobody wrote down.
  • Acceptance criteria: a first list from the user story. You add the edge cases production has taught you.
  • Release notes and changelogs: grouped by user impact. You cut anything only insiders care about.

Notice the pattern. The model does the arranging, and a person signs off on every claim about the real world.

Where it backfires

If the team accepts the first pass because it looks complete, AI made the work worse. If the team treats it as scaffolding, AI made the work easier to start. The model is the same in both cases. What differs is the review habit around it. Using AI without handing over your judgment goes deeper on keeping the final call.

Try this week

  • Pick one doc you've been putting off and ask for a plain first pass from your real notes, with [TODO] markers instead of guesses.
  • Add "no recommendation yet" to the prompt and see whether the discussion gets better.
  • Before you share the draft, highlight every claim and check each one against a source. Delete what you can't back up.
  • Try it on your next PR description and time how long your own pass takes.

Sometimes the best thing a fast tool can do is get you to the slow, careful part sooner. Let the model handle the first page and save your energy for the thinking.

faqs.q: What is a 'boring first pass' with AI?
faqs.a: A plain first draft that arranges your existing notes into structure: headings, claims, assumptions and open questions, with no persuasive polish. It exists so people can react to something concrete, and it's meant to be corrected.

faqs.q: Why not ask AI for a polished final version straight away?
faqs.a: Polish hides weak claims and makes a draft harder to criticize. A 2023 CHI study also found that an opinionated AI writing assistant shifted the views people expressed and their later attitudes, so a draft that takes a stance early can steer the decision. Ask for structure first and conclusions after the team has weighed in.

faqs.q: How much faster is drafting with AI?
faqs.a: In an MIT experiment published in Science in 2023, professionals using ChatGPT on writing tasks from their own jobs finished about 40% faster, with output rated 18% higher in quality. They also spent less time on rough drafting and more on ideas and editing. Your own gain depends on how much checking the draft needs.

faqs.q: What should a person always check in an AI first draft?
faqs.a: Every claim against its source, every example for whether it's real, trade-offs that got smoothed over, context only the team knows and anything that shouldn't be published. On tasks just outside what a model handles well, AI help can make answers worse, so a draft that looks good is no proof that it's right.
